questions.question: Which of the following festivals is celebrated primarily by the Parsi Community?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jashan-e-Mihragan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• **Jashan-e-Mihragan** is one of the most significant festivals celebrated by the Parsi community.

• The festival is dedicated to **Mithra**, the divinity of contracts, and is associated with the harvest season.

• It is a time for **thanksgiving** and sharing meals with family and friends, promoting social harmony and community bonding.

• The festival usually involves **ritual prayers, offerings, and festivities** that include music, dance, and traditional Parsi cuisine.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Parsi Community**

• The Parsi community is a Zoroastrian ethnic group who migrated to India from Persia (modern-day Iran) to escape religious persecution during the Islamic conquest.

• Zoroastrianism is one of the world's oldest continuously practiced religions, founded by the prophet Zoroaster in ancient Iran approximately 3,500 years ago.

• Parsis have greatly contributed to the economic, industrial, and cultural development of India, especially in Mumbai and Gujarat.

• **Songkran**

• Songkran is the Thai New Year festival celebrated primarily in Thailand.

• It is known for its water festival, where people splash water on each other to symbolize cleansing and renewal.

• **Milad-un-Nabi**

• Milad-un-Nabi is the celebration of the birth of the Prophet Muhammad, observed by Muslims around the world.

• The day is marked by prayers, sermons, and religious gatherings.

• **Deepawali**

• Deepawali, also known as Diwali, is a major Hindu festival celebrated by millions of people worldwide.

• It signifies the victory of light over darkness and good over evil, and involves lighting lamps, bursting firecrackers, and sharing sweets.

</ul

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT an effect of devaluation of the rupee in 1991 to make an international adjustment of Indian currency?

options.text: Raised the influx of foreign capital

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Increased imports**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• The devaluation of the rupee in 1991 was aimed at making Indian exports more competitive in the global market.

• The primary objective was to increase exports by reducing the cost of Indian goods in foreign markets.

• This devaluation also aimed to attract foreign capital inflows by making investments in India cheaper for foreign investors.

• Devaluation generally makes imports more expensive, thereby discouraging imports and encouraging domestic consumption.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Devaluation:**

• It refers to the deliberate downward adjustment of the value of a country's currency relative to another currency, group of currencies, or standard.

• Devaluation is a monetary policy tool used by countries that have a fixed exchange rate or semi-fixed exchange rate.

• The primary reasons for devaluation include boosting exports, reducing trade deficits, and attracting foreign investments.

• **Imports and Exports:**

• Imports are goods and services bought by residents of a country from another country. They are included in the calculation of a nation's GDP.

• Exports are goods and services produced in one country and sold to buyers in another. They are also a part of a country's GDP.

• Devaluation makes imports more expensive and exports cheaper, thereby aiming to correct trade imbalances.

• **Foreign Capital Inflows:**

• These are investments made by foreign entities into the domestic economy of a country.

• Such inflows can be in the form of direct investments, portfolio investments, and other financial instruments.

• Devaluation often makes a country’s assets cheaper for foreign investors, leading to an increase in foreign capital inflows.

• **1991 Economic Reforms in India:**

• In 1991, India faced a severe balance of payments crisis and implemented a series of economic reforms under the direction of the IMF and World Bank.

• The rupee was devalued as part of these reforms to address the immediate crisis and lay the foundation for economic liberalization.

• Other reforms included deregulation, reducing tariffs and interest rates, ending public monopolies, and initiating privatization.

questions.question: How many writs are guaranteed under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Five**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• Article 32 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to move to the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution.

• Article 32 provides for five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo-Warranto, and Certiorari.

• These writs are designed to enforce the fundamental rights of citizens against arbitrary actions of the state and other public authorities.

• Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the "heart and soul" of the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Habeas Corpus:**

• This writ is used to release a person who has been unlawfully detained or imprisoned.

• The term "Habeas Corpus" means "to have the body of".

• It is a powerful safeguard against arbitrary detention by the state.

• **Mandamus:**

• This writ is issued by a court to a public official or body to perform a duty they are obligated to perform.

• The term "Mandamus" means "we command".

• It ensures that duties imposed by law are fulfilled.

• **Prohibition:**

• This writ is issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to prevent it from exceeding its jurisdiction.

• The term "Prohibition" means "to forbid".

• It is used to stop lower courts from proceeding with cases they are not authorized to handle.

• **Quo-Warranto:**

• This writ is used to challenge the legality of a person's claim to a public office.

• The term "Quo-Warranto" means "by what authority".

• It helps ensure that public offices are not usurped by unauthorized persons.

• **Certiorari:**

• This writ is issued by a higher court to review the legality of a decision made by a lower court or tribunal.

• The term "Certiorari" means "to be certified" or "to be informed".

• It is used to correct errors in the proceedings of lower courts and tribunals.

</ul

questions.question: Who was the author of the book titled ‘Poverty and Un-British Rule in India’?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dadabhai Naoroji**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji** is often referred to as the Grand Old Man of India.
 
• He was the first Asian to be a British MP, representing the Finsbury Central constituency in London.
 
• Naoroji was a founding member of the Indian National Congress.
 
• His book, "**Poverty and Un-British Rule in India**", is a seminal text that highlighted the economic exploitation of India under British rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji:**

 
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji was an Indian political leader, merchant, scholar, and writer. He is known for his work in the Indian independence movement.
 
• He was instrumental in establishing the Indian National Congress and was its President three times.
 
• Naoroji's work and advocacy led to the appointment of the Welby Commission to investigate Indian finances.
 
• He also played a significant role in the founding of the London Indian Society and the East India Association, both of which aimed at raising awareness of Indian issues in Britain.
 
 
 
• **Poverty and Un-British Rule in India:**
 
 
• This book, published in 1901, is one of Naoroji's most important works. It analyzed the economic impacts of British rule in India.
 
• The book argued that British policies were causing widespread poverty in India by draining wealth from the country.
 
• Naoroji introduced the concept of the "drain theory," which posited that the British were extracting wealth from India to benefit Britain, leading to the impoverishment of India.
 
• The book was influential in shaping Indian nationalist thought and provided a strong intellectual foundation for the Indian independence movement.
 
 
 
• **Indian National Congress:**
 
 
• The Indian National Congress (INC) is a political party in India, founded in 1885. It played a major role in the Indian independence movement.
 
• Key leaders of the INC included Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
 
• The INC was instrumental in organizing mass protests, civil disobedience, and non-violent resistance against British rule.
 
• Post-independence, the INC became the dominant political party in India, leading the country for several decades.
 
 
 
• **British Rule in India:**
 
 
• The British East India Company began its trade operations in India in the early 17th century and gradually expanded its control over the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Following the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the British Crown took direct control of India, leading to the establishment of the British Raj.
 
• British policies in India were often exploitative, focusing on extracting resources and wealth for the benefit of Britain.
 
• The economic, social, and political impact of British rule led to significant changes in Indian society and laid the groundwork for the independence movement.

questions.question: Vijayalaya, who belonged to the ancient chiefly family of the Cholas from Uraiyur, captured the delta from the Muttaraiyar in the middle of the 9th century and built the town of ______________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Thanjavur**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• Thanjavur, also known as Tanjore, was a major city of the Chola dynasty.

• Vijayalaya Chola, the founder of the imperial Chola dynasty, captured Thanjavur in the middle of the 9th century.

• Thanjavur became the capital of the Cholas during the reign of Vijayalaya Chola.

• Thanjavur is renowned for its rich cultural heritage, particularly during the Chola period, which saw the construction of the famous Brihadeeswarar Temple.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Vijayalaya Chola:**

• Vijayalaya Chola was the founder of the Chola dynasty that would go on to become one of the longest-ruling dynasties in the history of southern India.

• Before Vijayalaya's reign, the Cholas were chieftains and had lost their prominence to the Pallavas and Pandyas.

• Vijayalaya's capture of Thanjavur marked the revival of the Chola dynasty.

• **Muttaraiyar:**

• The Muttaraiyar were a dynasty of feudatories who ruled over the Tanjore region before the rise of the Cholas.

• Vijayalaya Chola defeated the Muttaraiyar to capture Thanjavur, setting the stage for the expansion of the Chola Empire.

• **Chola Dynasty:**

• The Chola dynasty was a Tamil dynasty that ruled primarily in southern India until the 13th century.

• The Cholas are well-known for their contributions to art, architecture, and administration.

• Some of the most remarkable architectural feats of the Cholas include the Brihadeeswarar Temple and the Gangaikonda Cholapuram Temple.

• **Thanjavur (Tanjore):**

• Thanjavur is located in the Indian state of Tamil Nadu.

• It was the capital city during the reign of the Chola dynasty and later the Nayak kingdom.

• Thanjavur is an important center of South Indian religion, art, and architecture, with the Brihadeeswarar Temple being a UNESCO World Heritage site.

</ul

questions.question: Totaram Sharma, Pandit Ayodhya Prasad, Gopal Das and Babu Ram Shanker Pagaldas are noted players of which of the following instruments?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pakhawaj**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• **Pakhawaj** is a barrel-shaped drum traditionally used in Hindustani classical music.

• The instrument is similar to the **mridangam**, which is used in Carnatic classical music.

• It is played horizontally and usually accompanies the **dhrupad** style of singing.

• The Pakhawaj is known for its deep, resonant sound and is made of wood with a leather drumhead on each end.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Sarod**

• The Sarod is a stringed instrument used mainly in Indian classical music.

• It is known for its deep, weighty, introspective sound and is an important concert instrument in Hindustani music.

• The Sarod is played with a plectrum made of coconut shell, and the strings are pressed with the fingernails to produce a clear sound.

• **Mridangam**

• The Mridangam is a percussion instrument originating from South India.

• It is the primary rhythmic accompaniment in a Carnatic music ensemble.

• The Mridangam is an ancient instrument and is considered the precursor to the Pakhawaj.

• **Sarangi**

• The Sarangi is a bowed, short-necked string instrument from India.

• It is an important instrument in Hindustani classical music and is known for its ability to mimic the human voice.

• The Sarangi has three main playing strings and a number of sympathetic strings that resonate along with the played notes.

</ul

questions.question: In Ancient India, which of the following dynasties was empowered in Deccan by Gautamiputra Satakarni?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Satavahana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• The Satavahana dynasty was an Indian dynasty based in the Deccan region.

• Gautamiputra Satakarni was one of the most powerful rulers of the Satavahana dynasty.

• He reigned in the early 2nd century CE and significantly expanded the Satavahana territory.

• Gautamiputra Satakarni is known for his military conquests and his efforts to revive Vedic traditions and culture.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Satavahana Dynasty**

• The Satavahana dynasty, also known as the Andhras, ruled the Deccan region of India from approximately the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE.

• Their capital was Pratishthana (modern-day Paithan in Maharashtra).

• The dynasty is noted for its contribution to Indian art, culture, and trade. They played a significant role in promoting Buddhism.

• The Satavahanas issued the first known Indian coins with portraits of their rulers, which influenced later Indian coinage.

• **Gautamiputra Satakarni**

• Gautamiputra Satakarni is often regarded as the greatest of the Satavahana kings.

• His reign is marked by the successful defense of the Deccan region against foreign invasions, particularly from the Sakas (Western Kshatrapas).

• He is celebrated for his revival of Vedic sacrifices and his efforts to restore the traditional social order.

• His achievements are recorded in the Nasik inscription by his mother, Gautami Balashri.

• **Deccan Region**

• The Deccan region refers to the large plateau in western and southern India, bounded by the Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats.

• This region has historically been a significant center of Indian culture and political power, with various dynasties ruling over it.

• The Satavahanas, Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, and Vijayanagara Empire are some of the notable dynasties that ruled the Deccan.

• The Deccan is known for its unique contributions to Indian architecture, literature, and art.

</ul

questions.question: In which year was the Basketball Federation of India established?

The correct answer is __**1950**__.

questions.question: Who among the following Gurus of Sikh religion was the last Guru?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Guru Gobind Singh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Guru Gobind Singh was the **10th and last of the Sikh Gurus**.
 
• He was born on **22 December 1666** in Patna, Bihar, India.
 
• Guru Gobind Singh founded the **Khalsa in 1699**, which played a significant role in the religious and military history of the Sikhs.
 
• He introduced the **Five Ks (Kesh, Kangha, Kara, Kachera, Kirpan)**, which are the five articles of faith that Khalsa Sikhs must wear at all times.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Guru Angad**

 
 
• He was the **second Sikh Guru**, succeeding Guru Nanak.
 
• Guru Angad is credited with **standardizing the Gurmukhi script**, which became the script for the Punjabi language.
 
 
 
• **Guru Amar Das**
 
 
• He was the **third Sikh Guru**.
 
• Guru Amar Das is known for establishing **Manji and Piri systems of religious administration** in Sikhism.
 
• He also started the tradition of **Langar** (community kitchen) in Sikh temples.
 
 
 
• **Guru Hargobind**
 
 
• He was the **sixth Sikh Guru**.
 
• Guru Hargobind is notable for introducing the concept of **Miri and Piri** (temporal and spiritual authority).
 
• He wore two swords, representing both temporal and spiritual power.
 
 
 
• **Guru Gobind Singh**
 
 
• He was the **tenth and last Sikh Guru**.
 
• Guru Gobind Singh initiated the Khalsa and declared the **Guru Granth Sahib** as the eternal Guru of the Sikhs after him.

questions.question: The decennial census of India is conducted under which Census Act?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Census Act 1948**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Census Act 1948 provides the legal framework for conducting the decennial Census in India.
 
• It was enacted by the Parliament of India to ensure the systematic collection of demographic data.
 
• The act empowers the government to conduct the census and collect demographic information such as population size, growth, density, and other vital statistics.
 
• The Census of India is conducted every 10 years, and it is one of the most extensive administrative exercises in the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Decennial Census:**

 
 
• The decennial census is a comprehensive exercise conducted every ten years to gather demographic data about the population of a country.
 
• It includes data on population size, density, growth rate, age distribution, sex ratio, literacy rate, and other socio-economic factors.
 
• This data is crucial for planning and policy-making by the government.
 
 
 
• **Census Act 1948:**
 
 
• The Census Act 1948 was enacted to provide the legal foundation for conducting the census in India.
 
• The act outlines the duties and responsibilities of census officers and the procedures for data collection and confidentiality.
 
• It ensures that the data collected during the census is used solely for statistical purposes and is kept confidential.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Census:**
 
 
• The census data is vital for the government to allocate resources, plan infrastructure, and implement various welfare schemes effectively.
 
• It helps in identifying demographic trends and making informed decisions for the socio-economic development of the country.
 
• The data is used for electoral constituency delimitation, urban planning, and understanding population dynamics.

questions.question: According to Census of India 2011, which union territories have the lowest literacy rate?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dadra and Nagar Haveli**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Dadra and Nagar Haveli had the lowest literacy rate among the Union Territories as per the Census of India 2011.
 
• The literacy rate of Dadra and Nagar Haveli was recorded at 76.2%.
 
• In comparison, Chandigarh had a literacy rate of 86.05%, Lakshadweep had a literacy rate of 92.28%, and Andaman and Nicobar had a literacy rate of 86.27%.
 
• The literacy rate is a key indicator of the socio-economic progress of a region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Census of India**

 
 
• The Census of India is a decennial exercise conducted by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India under the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.
 
• It provides a comprehensive account of the demographic, social, and economic profile of the country.
 
• The first census in India was conducted in 1872, and since then, it has been carried out every ten years.
 
• The Census of India 2011 was the 15th National Census since 1872 and the 7th census after independence.
 
 
 
• **Literacy Rate**
 
 
• The literacy rate is defined as the percentage of people who can read and write with understanding in a given language.
 
• It is an important indicator of the educational status of a population.
 
• Literacy has a significant impact on various socio-economic factors including employment, income levels, health, and overall quality of life.
 
• Higher literacy rates are often associated with better economic development and improved social outcomes.
 
 
 
• **Union Territories of India**
 
 
• India is divided into states and Union Territories (UTs).
 
• Union Territories are regions governed directly by the Central Government of India.
 
• As of 2021, India has 8 Union Territories: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Lakshadweep, Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.
 
• Each Union Territory has its own unique cultural, demographic, and socio-economic profile.

questions.question: In Indo Islamic construction, _________and lime mortar was an important factor in construction.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**concrete**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• Concrete is a versatile building material composed of aggregate (gravel, sand, or rock), cement, and water.

• Its strength and durability make it a preferred choice for construction, particularly in Indo-Islamic architecture.

• Lime mortar, used in conjunction with concrete, improves workability and strength.

• Indo-Islamic architecture often featured intricate designs and structures that necessitated the use of robust materials like concrete.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Concrete**

• Concrete is made by mixing cement, water, and aggregates (gravel, sand, or crushed stone).

• It is known for its high compressive strength, making it suitable for building structures like bridges, buildings, and roads.

• Concrete can be molded into various shapes and sizes before it hardens, allowing for a wide range of architectural designs.

• It has a long lifespan and requires minimal maintenance, contributing to its widespread use in construction.

• **Lime Mortar**

• Lime mortar is a traditional building material made by mixing lime, sand, and water.

• It has been used for centuries and is known for its flexibility, breathability, and ability to self-heal small cracks.

• Lime mortar is particularly beneficial in historic building conservation due to its compatibility with older structures.

• It provides a durable and stable binding material for masonry work, enhancing the longevity of buildings.

• **Indo-Islamic Architecture**

• Indo-Islamic architecture emerged in the Indian subcontinent under the influence of Islamic rule.

• It is characterized by features such as domes, minarets, arches, and intricate ornamentation.

• Notable examples include the Qutub Minar, Taj Mahal, and various Mughal-era forts and palaces.

• The use of durable materials like concrete and lime mortar was crucial in creating these enduring architectural masterpieces.

</ul

questions.question: As of November 2022, in which of the following periods in Indian history was the Republic Day parade NOT performed at the Rajpath(now called Kartavya Path)?

questions.question: Which method is used to separate ribosomes from the cell?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ultracentrifugation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• Ultracentrifugation is a technique used to separate particles based on their size, shape, and density by spinning them at high speeds.

• This method can achieve very high centrifugal forces, making it ideal for separating subcellular components like ribosomes.

• The process involves spinning the sample at speeds typically greater than 20,000 revolutions per minute (RPM).

• Ultracentrifugation is widely used in molecular biology, biochemistry, and cell biology for the isolation and purification of organelles and macromolecules.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Chromatography**

• Chromatography is a laboratory technique for the separation of a mixture into its individual components.

• It is based on the differential partitioning between the mobile phase and the stationary phase.

• This method is not typically used for separating cell organelles like ribosomes.

• **Distillation**

• Distillation is a process used to separate components of a mixture based on differences in their boiling points.

• It is commonly used for purifying liquids and is not suitable for separating cellular organelles.

• **Filtration**

• Filtration is a physical or mechanical process used to separate solids from liquids or gases using a filter medium.

• This method is useful for separating large particles but is not effective for isolating smaller cellular components like ribosomes.

• **Ultracentrifugation**

• As explained, ultracentrifugation is highly effective for the separation of small subcellular components such as ribosomes.

</ul

questions.question: Which of the following causes the Tsunami waves?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Interior of the earth**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• Earthquakes occurring under the sea or ocean floor are the primary cause of tsunami waves.

• These seismic activities result in a sudden displacement of a large volume of water, generating waves that travel across the ocean at high speeds.

• Volcanic eruptions and underwater landslides can also contribute to the formation of tsunamis.

• The energy released by these geological activities within the earth’s interior can displace water vertically, creating waves that can travel long distances and cause significant damage upon reaching coastal areas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Tsunami**

• A tsunami is a series of ocean waves with extremely long wavelengths caused by large-scale disturbances of the ocean, such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or underwater landslides.

• When the ocean floor abruptly deforms and displaces the overlying water, it triggers a series of waves that can travel across entire ocean basins.

• Tsunamis are different from normal sea waves as their wavelengths are much longer, and they travel at much higher speeds.

• In deep water, tsunami waves may not be noticeable, but as they approach shallower coastal areas, they can increase in height dramatically and cause widespread destruction.

• **Earthquake**

• An earthquake is the shaking of the surface of the Earth resulting from a sudden release of energy in the Earth's lithosphere that creates seismic waves.

• Earthquakes can range in size from those that are so weak that they cannot be felt to those violent enough to toss people around and destroy whole cities.

• The seismicity, or seismic activity, of an area refers to the frequency, type, and size of earthquakes experienced over a period of time.

• **Volcanic Eruption**

• A volcanic eruption occurs when magma from beneath the Earth's crust is expelled through a volcano.

• Eruptions can release lava, ash, and gases that can cause widespread damage and affect global climates.

• Underwater volcanic eruptions can displace water and generate tsunamis.

• **Underwater Landslide**

• Underwater landslides, or submarine landslides, occur when sediments on the continental shelf or slope become destabilized and move downslope under the influence of gravity.

• These landslides can trigger tsunamis by displacing large volumes of water.

• Basaltic magma is typically generated in the upper mantle due to partial melting of peridotite.

• Geological processes such as decompression melting and the addition of volatiles can cause the formation of basaltic magma in this region.

• This region is characterized by significant changes in mineral phases due to increasing pressure.

• **Lower mantle**

• The lower mantle lies between the transition region and the core-mantle boundary, extending from 660 kilometers to about 2,900 kilometers in depth.

• It is composed of minerals such as bridgmanite and ferropericlase, which are stable at high pressures.

• Basaltic magma does not typically originate in the lower mantle due to the extreme pressures and different mineral compositions.

__
 
• **Part IV** of the Indian Constitution specifically deals with the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
 
• The Directive Principles of State Policy are guidelines for the framing of laws by the government.
 
• These principles are considered fundamental in the governance of the country and aim to create a social order characterized by social, economic, and political justice.
 
• They are non-justiciable in nature, meaning they are not enforceable by any court, but the principles laid down are considered essential in the governance of the country.

• The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in Articles 36 to 51 in Part IV of the Indian Constitution.
 
• They are borrowed from the Irish Constitution and are meant to establish a welfare state where the government works towards the well-being of its citizens.
 
• DPSPs are classified into three categories: Socialistic, Gandhian, and Liberal-Intellectual principles.
 
• Examples of DPSPs include provisions for securing the right to work, education, and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, and disablement (Article 41), and promotion of educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and other weaker sections (Article 46).
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights**
 
 
• Contained in Part III (Articles 12 to 35) of the Indian Constitution, Fundamental Rights are basic human rights guaranteed to all citizens.
 
• These rights are justiciable, meaning they are enforceable by the courts.
 
• Fundamental Rights include the right to equality, right to freedom, right against exploitation, right to freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and the right to constitutional remedies.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Duties**
 
 
• Listed in Part IV-A (Article 51A) of the Indian Constitution, Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
 
• These duties are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by the courts.
 
• Fundamental Duties include abiding by the Constitution, respecting the national flag and the national anthem, protecting the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India, and promoting harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood among all the people of India.

• Part XX of the Indian Constitution deals with the amendment of the Constitution, covered under Article 368.

• It provides the procedure for amending the Constitution, including the requirements for a special majority in Parliament.

• Part XV of the Indian Constitution deals with elections, covering Articles 324 to 329A.

• It includes provisions related to the Election Commission, conduct of elections, and matters related to electoral rolls.

questions.question: Which of the following is INCORRECT with respect to repo rate?

options.text: It is a single policy rate to signal the stance of monetary policy to achieve macro-economic objectives of growth with price stability
It is a policy rate which is the key lending rate of the central bank, and its nomenclature varies from country to country.
It is the rate at which banks place their funds with the RBI and receive collateral.
It is the rate at which the commercial banks borrow funds from the RBI.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**option 3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• The repo rate is a single policy rate used by central banks to signal the stance of monetary policy to achieve macro-economic objectives of growth with price stability.

• The repo rate is a key lending rate of the central bank, and its nomenclature varies from country to country.

• The repo rate is the rate at which commercial banks borrow funds from the RBI (Reserve Bank of India).

• The incorrect statement is that the repo rate is the rate at which banks place their funds with the RBI and receive collateral. This describes the reverse repo rate, not the repo rate.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Repo Rate:**

• The repo rate, or repurchase rate, is the rate at which the central bank of a country (RBI in India) lends money to commercial banks in the event of any shortfall of funds.

• The repo rate is used by monetary authorities to control inflation. When inflation is high, central banks increase the repo rate to discourage banks from borrowing, which reduces the money supply in the economy.

• Conversely, when the central bank wants to inject funds into the system, it lowers the repo rate, making borrowing cheaper for banks.

• It is a crucial instrument of monetary policy and is used to maintain liquidity and control inflation in the economy.

• **Reverse Repo Rate:**

• It is the rate at which the central bank borrows money from commercial banks within the country.

• It is a monetary policy instrument which can be used to control the money supply in the country.

• The reverse repo rate is an instrument to absorb the liquidity in the market, thereby tightening the money supply.

• When the reverse repo rate is increased, it encourages banks to park their surplus funds with the central bank, thus absorbing excess liquidity from the banking system.

• **Monetary Policy:**

• Monetary policy refers to the policy adopted by the monetary authority of a country to control either the interest rate payable on very short-term borrowing or the money supply.

• It is a key tool used to achieve macroeconomic objectives such as controlling inflation, consumption, growth, and liquidity.

• In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is responsible for formulating and implementing monetary policy.

• Key instruments of monetary policy include the repo rate, reverse repo rate, cash reserve ratio (CRR), and statutory liquidity ratio (SLR).

</ul

questions.question: Alarmel Valli and Rukmini Devi Arundale are associated with which of the following styles of Indian Dances?

• Examples include wheat, barley, peas, gram, and mustard.

questions.question: Net national product at market price can be defined as:

options.text: Gross national product at market price plus depreciation
Net domestic product at market price plus net income from abroad
Net domestic product at market price minus net income from abroad
Net domestic product at market price minus depreciation

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Net domestic product at market price plus net income from abroad**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• **Net National Product (NNP) at market price** is calculated by adjusting the Net Domestic Product (NDP) at market price with the net income from abroad.

• **Net income from abroad** includes the difference between the income residents earn from abroad and the income that foreigners earn within the domestic economy.

• The formula for NNP at market price is: **NNP at market price = NDP at market price + Net income from abroad**.

• It reflects the overall economic performance of a country considering both domestic and international income.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Gross National Product (GNP):**

• GNP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced by the residents of a country in a given period, usually a year.

• It includes the income earned by residents from abroad but excludes the income earned by foreigners within the domestic economy.

• **Net Domestic Product (NDP):**

• NDP is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period, minus depreciation.

• It reflects the actual economic output, accounting for the wear and tear on the capital stock.

• **Depreciation:**

• Depreciation represents the reduction in the value of an asset over time due to wear and tear, age, or obsolescence.

• In national accounting, it is subtracted from the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to calculate the NDP.

• **Net Income from Abroad:**

• It is the difference between the income earned by residents from their investments abroad and the income earned by foreigners from their investments in the domestic economy.

• This component is crucial in adjusting the domestic product to reflect the true economic performance of a nation on a global scale.

</ul
